props.title: Somersault

sections.content: Somersault marked a watershed moment in Australian cinema, launching Abbie Cornish's career and establishing Cate Shortland as a major directorial voice. The film's raw exploration of teenage sexuality and identity through 16-year-old Heidi's journey to the ski town of Jindabyne created a new visual language for Australian coming-of-age stories. Its influence can be seen in later works like 52 Tuesdays (2013) and Looking for Grace (2015), establishing a template for intimate character studies that prioritize emotional authenticity over plot mechanics.

sections.content: The film's visual style, with its heightened sensory elements and intimate close-ups, influenced a generation of Australian filmmakers. Shortland's approach shares DNA with Sleeping Beauty (2011) and Beautiful Kate (2009), other Australian films that deal with female sexuality and awakening. The use of color and texture to convey emotional states became a hallmark of this new wave of Australian cinema, seeing echoes in works like Breath (2017) and Babyteeth (2019).

Sam Worthington's nuanced performance as Joe, a young man struggling with his own sexuality and identity, prefigured his later stardom and represents a type of masculine vulnerability rarely seen in Australian cinema of the period. This character complexity influenced later Australian male characterizations in films like Holding the Man (2015) and The Boys Are Back (2009). SUBHEAD: Impact on Contemporary Australian Cinema

sections.content: Shortland's intimate directing style in Somersault created a template for depicting complex female characters that influenced films like Little Fish (2005) and Blessed (2009). The film's success at Cannes helped pave the way for other Australian directors exploring similar themes, including The Daughter (2015) and Girl Asleep (2015), which share its dreamy, subjective approach to storytelling.
